#### Summary

In recent years, Latin America has experienced a rightward shift as voters have turned against incumbent left-wing governments. The trend began in Argentina in 2023, when Javier Milei defeated the Peronist governing coalition, and continued in Bolivia, Chile and Honduras in 2025, where left-led governments lost power. In 2026, the trend continued with Keiko Fujimori’s victory in Peru, while Abelardo De La Espriella’s election in Colombia brought the country’s brief experience of left-wing government to an end.

These electoral shifts also align with the Trump administration’s explicitly stated ambitions for the region. The US National Security Strategy published in November 2025 calls for Washington to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere” and pledges to “reward and encourage” governments, parties and movements broadly aligned with US principles and strategy [@whitehouse2025, 15]. Trump has also intervened overtly in several electoral campaigns by publicly endorsing ideologically aligned candidates, including in Colombia, Chile and Honduras, and backing Javier Milei’s political camp ahead of Argentina’s 2025 mid-term elections. “Lots of people that I got elected”, he said in September 2026 [@bloomfield_trump_south_america_2026]. However, these interventions do not by themselves explain the region’s political trajectory. ECLAC’s comparative analysis of 16 Latin American countries found that, between 2015 and 2025, incumbent parties or coalitions lost 74 per cent of presidential elections, compared with 44 per cent between 2003 and 2014 [@salazar_xirinachs_boeninger_2026_endogenous_governance]. Recent continuity cases include Mexico, Paraguay, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador and Ecuador, as well as Costa Rica, where Laura Fernández promised continuity with Rodrigo Chaves. The pattern therefore suggests that the current rightward shift is driven in significant part by a broader cycle of anti-incumbency, in which voters punish governments for perceived failures to deliver on security, economic conditions and other immediate concerns. Since voters have increasingly turned against incumbent left-wing governments in favour of anti-establishment challengers, often radical right-wing or far-right outsiders, this discontent has frequently translated into a shift to the right. US endorsements and political pressure may reinforce that shift, but they are not sufficient to explain it.

### Argentina

Argentina’s political trajectory since 2000 has been shaped by recurring economic crises and shifts between governments pursuing different economic models. In 2001, President Fernando de la Rúa’s government imposed the *corralito*, severely restricting withdrawals from bank accounts amid a financial collapse and the subsequent conversion of dollars deposits (a common practice among Argentines to keep savings in dollars due to the volatiliy of the pesos) into pesos at an unfavourable exchange rate. These measures fuelled mass protests and riots that forced him to resign. The crisis paved the way for the election of Néstor Kirchner in 2003, whose Peronist government pursued a more interventionist, centre-left agenda, continued under his wife Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who succeeded him as president in 2007 following his decision not to seek re-election. Her administrations expanded state involvement in the economy and social spending. In 2015, centre-right candidate Mauricio Macri won the presidency promising market-oriented reforms and closer ties with Western economies. In 2018, Macri's government secured a US\$ 57 billion IMF programme, the largest in the Fund's history. The arrangement was widely criticised as political support for Macri ahead of the 2019 presidential election as most of the funds were disbursed before the elections [@green_2020_argentina_imf_reelection]. The programme failed to restore economic stability and Macri lost to Peronist candidate Alberto Fernández.

In the 2023 elections, Javier Milei won a resounding victory against the economy minister of Alberto Fernández, Sergio Massa. Fernández did not stand for re-election due to his high impopularity. During Fernández's government, annual inflation had reached 138 per cent, and Milei's promise to bring it under control found fertile ground among voters desperate for change. His win marked the beginning of a dramatic ideological shift in Argentina and the wider region; which had been dominated by left-wing governments for much of the preceding decade. Milei describes himself as an "anarcho-capitalist" who sees the state as the enemy and vowed to dismantle what he calls the political caste. His win also marked the beginning of Argentina's closer realignment with the US.

Milei triumphed again at the midterm elections in October 2025, with his party securing a majority in the legislature. Prior to those elections, the US announced considerable financial assistance to shore up Argentina's economy (an up to \$40 billion bailout package), and President Trump made clear he would consider rescinding it in the event of an opposition victory. While Milei succeeded in bringing inflation under control, the social cost of deep cuts to public spending has dented his initial popularity. His image as an anti-corruption candidate has also taken severe blows, as Milei himself and members of his inner circle have been accused of illicit enrichment. His spokesperson and head of cabinet, Manuel Adorni, was compelled to resign at the end of June 2026 after failing to account for the origin of his sudden and substantial wealth.

In December 2023, Milei rejected the invitation, received during his predecessor's mandate, to join the enlarged BRICS+ bloc. While during his campaign he vowed to sever all ties with Communist China, this has not materialised in practice given Argentina's reliance on China as a major trading partner and source of financial support, including a significant currency swap line with the People's Bank of China. Milei's administration has also not formally withdrawn from China’s Belt and Road Initiative, which Argentina joined in 2022 with pledges of over \$23 billion in Chinese financing and investment. However, criticism of China and its Communist leadership continues among members of the administration. On 30 August 2026, shortly after the devastating floods and landslides on the Nepal-China border, the National Director of Digital Communication, Juan Pablo Carreira @carreira_2026_china , published a post on X blaming the management of the Communist Party for the disaster, provoking a formal rebuke from the Chinese embassy [-@chinaembarg_2026_declaracion] in Buenos Aires.

The next general elections are scheduled for October 2027. Most polls still show Milei ahead, but his political popularity has reached its lowest point since taking office. This context may help explain why the long-standing dispute over the islands known to Britain as the Falklands and to Argentina as the Malvinas has resurfaced on the political agenda. Similar to 1982, when the military junta, facing growing domestic opposition amid mass disappearances and widespread human rights abuses, decided to seize the islands from the United Kingdom, triggering a brief but bloody conflict, it is tempting to see the Malvinas question resurfacing on the political agenda as serving similar domestic political purposes [@tait2026_Trump_Falklands]. Adding a new dimension to the dispute, Trump has signalled that he may reconsider the traditional US position supporting British sovereignty, reportedly as leverage against NATO allies that declined to join the Iran war, while simultaneously seeking to reward partners in the Western Hemisphere.

### Belize

Since 2000, Belizean politics has been dominated by alternating governments from the two main parties: the People’s United Party (PUP), broadly associated with the centre-left, and the United Democratic Party (UDP), generally considered centre-right. The PUP government of Said Musa, in office since 1998, won re-election in 2003 but was defeated in 2008 by the UDP under Dean Barrow, following growing concerns about corruption, public debt and economic management. The UDP retained power in 2012 and 2015, before the PUP under John Briceño returned to office in 2020. Briceño won a second consecutive term in March 2025, with the PUP retaining 26 of the 31 seats in parliament while a divided UDP contested the election in rival factions. Although the parties occupy different positions on the political spectrum, Belize has not experienced the sharp ideological swings seen elsewhere in Latin America. While ideology and ethnicity help explain party allegiance, clientelism remains a central feature of the party system and a key mechanism for sustaining electoral loyalty [@ferrell_wainwright_2023_belize_political_economy; @perello_navia_2025_belize_clientelism; @ipu_2008_belize_elections].

Belize continues to face challenges associated with organised crime, including gang violence, economic dependence on tourism and limited state capacity. A longstanding foreign-policy and security concern is Guatemala’s territorial claim over approximately 53 per cent of Belize’s land territory, which the two countries agreed to submit to the International Court of Justice. Belize’s case illustrates how a small state relies on international law and multilateral institutions to manage disputes that could otherwise threaten its sovereignty. Meanwhile, the 2025 election exposed the weakness of the parliamentary opposition, with the UDP split contributing to another decisive PUP victory. The political system remains competitive, but the dominance of two established parties and the importance of patronage networks raise questions about the scope for new political alternatives [@perello_navia_2025_belize_clientelism; @ferrell_wainwright_2023_belize_political_economy; @greater_belize_media_2026_icj_hearings].

Relations with the United States are particularly important because of trade, tourism, migration (the US is home to roughly one-third of all Belizeans) and security cooperation [@ferrell_wainwright_2023_belize_political_economy]. In October 2025, Briceño’s government signed a US asylum-cooperation agreement under which eligible third-country nationals seeking protection in the United States can be transferred to Belize to have their claims examined. The arrangement became operational in July 2026, though initial transfers involved only a small number of individuals [@janetsky_2025_belize_safe_third_country; @love_fm_2026_belize_safe_third_country_transfers]. Belize was absent from Trump’s *Shield of the Americas* summit in March 2026 as the country had not been invited, so its absence should not be described as a refusal to join. The exclusion is nevertheless noteworthy given the administration’s emphasis on building a selective coalition of regional governments around security and countering Chinese influence [@greater_belize_media_2026_shield_not_invited].

Belize’s most consequential geopolitical commitment is its continued diplomatic recognition of Taiwan, with which it has maintained relations since 1989. It is one of a dwindling group of twelve countries worldwide that retain formal diplomatic ties with Taipei and has no diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China. The relationship has brought cooperation in development, health, education, infrastructure and agriculture, but it has also exposed Belize to pressure from Beijing. On 12 October 2026, China sanctioned Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca over his country’s support for Taiwan, imposing entry restrictions on him in Hong Kong and Macau and prohibiting Chinese organisations and individuals from cooperating with him. Washington condemned China’s actions as coercive [@lee_blanchard_2026_china_sanctions_belize_taiwan; @reuters_2026_us_opposes_china_coercion].

Belize therefore combines conventional two-party electoral competition with a foreign policy shaped by the constraints of a small state. Its domestic politics has been shaped more by party networks, clientelism and governance than by sharp ideological shifts. Internationally, its ties with Taiwan place it on one side of an increasingly contentious diplomatic divide, while its security and migration cooperation with the United States remains important. At the same time, the government's exclusion from the *Shield of the Americas* illustrates that close bilateral relations do not guarantee inclusion in Washington’s preferred regional initiatives.

### Bolivia

Bolivia’s political landscape was transformed in the early 2000s by a wave of social mobilisation rooted in deep inequalities between the country’s largely mestizo and white urban elite and its majority indigenous population, which had been systematically excluded from political and economic power since independence. The so-called Water War of 2000 in Cochabamba, triggered by the privatisation of the city’s water supply, and the Gas War of 2003, which led to the resignation and flight into exile of President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada, marked the collapse of the traditional party system and opened the door for a new political force [@climatediplomacy_cochabamba]. Sánchez de Lozada, a US-educated mining magnate who had presided over a privatisation programme and oversaw a violent crackdown on protesters that left more than sixty people dead, was succeeded by his vice-president Carlos Mesa, who in turn resigned in 2005 under renewed popular pressure. Into this political vacuum stepped Evo Morales, a coca growers’ union leader from the Chapare region and a member of the Aymara people, who had built the Movement Toward Socialism (*Movimiento al Socialismo*, MAS) as a vehicle for Bolivia’s long-marginalised indigenous majority. In December 2005, Morales won the presidential election with 53.7 per cent of the vote in the first round, an outright majority unprecedented in Bolivian electoral history, becoming the country’s first indigenous head of state. He oversaw a new Constitution in 2009 that formally recognised Bolivia as a plurinational state and enshrined the rights of indigenous peoples. His governments pursued a programme of nationalisation of the hydrocarbons sector, expanded social programmes, and presided over a sustained reduction in poverty and inequality during a period of high commodity prices.

After nearly two decades of political dominance by the MAS, interrupted only briefly in 2019-2020 when Morales resigned and went into exile following disputed elections and military pressure, three presidential terms under his leadership and one by Luis Arce, the 2025 general elections marked a significant political shift with the election of Rodrigo Paz, son of former president Jaime Paz Zamora. Paz is a social conservative who advocates free market reforms and “capitalism for all.”

Bolivia is an ethnically diverse country in which roughly half the population is of indigenous origin, a group that had long formed the backbone of the MAS movement. However, internal divisions within the party led to a fragmentation of the MAS vote in the 2025 elections, as several younger candidates competed for that same electorate. Paz managed to attract a share of the indigenous vote through his running mate, Edmand Lara, a former police officer who had gained public prominence through his exposure of corruption on social media. This alliance proved decisive in the second round, as no other candidate had indigenous roots. It did not last long, however. Shortly after the election, Lara declared himself in opposition to the government.

Morales, who retains strong support among part of the population, presided over a period of economic growth and poverty reduction largely financed by high commodity prices, particularly hydrocarbons. This economic boom came to an abrupt end in 2023, when Bolivia entered a severe economic crisis characterised by a foreign exchange shortage, a sharp decline in international reserves, a structural fiscal deficit, and growing pressure on the national currency, the boliviano. Against this backdrop, the ruling MAS party became engulfed in an open power struggle between then-president Luis Arce and former president Morales, who was subsequently expelled from the party.

Despite a constitutional term limit on standing for re-election, Morales sought to advance his candidacy for the 2025 race, though his bid was ultimately rejected. He initially called for disruption of the electoral process, triggering sporadic violence across the country, before shifting to promoting a protest vote during the first-round campaign. He remains in hiding in the Chapare coca-growing region, where he commands strong social support, as multiple arrest warrants place him at risk of detention. He is facing a human-trafficking case related to allegations that he fathered a child with a fifteen-year-old girl during his presidency; having failed to appear at trial, a further arrest warrant was issued. The case dates to 2020, during the brief interim presidency of opposition leader Jeanine Áñez. Morales' legal team has characterised it as political persecution [@ruvenal_2026_morales]. In October 2026, another charge was added as Bolivia's attorney general announced an investigation into Morales' alleged involvement in the murder and torture of European citizens in 2009 [@afp_2026_bolivia_morales_2009_killings].

When Paz moved to slash long-standing fuel subsidies in order to reduce the budget deficit, widespread protests erupted, culminating in fifty days of highway blockades by labour unions and indigenous groups that brought the country to a standstill and pushed the government to the brink of collapse. The blockades had a cascading effect on the economy and society, with soaring prices putting basic goods out of reach for many Bolivians and hospitals facing shortages of medicines. The situation was brought to an end after Paz declared a state of emergency and authorised greater military involvement in restoring road access. Morales backed the protests, leading to a new arrest warrant issued in July 2026 for alleged armed uprising against the state. In light of the rising social discontent, Morales told journalists that he is contemplating a return to politics [@garrison_2026_morales].

On the foreign policy front, Paz has overseen a significant reorientation of Bolivia towards Washington after nearly two decades of strained relations under Morales, who famously expelled the US ambassador, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and USAID. Paz lifted visa requirements for US citizens, welcomed back a US ambassador, secured multilateral financing including from the Washington-based Inter-American Development Bank, and invited the DEA to resume operations in the country. He has also courted US technology giants such as Amazon, Tesla, and Oracle to invest in Bolivia's lithium and rare earth mineral industries [@swift2026_NYT].

The arrest of Fernando Cerimedo on 18 August in Bolivia, on charges of allegedly plotting to kill his girlfriend, Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller, had far-reaching political consequences, given that he had served as a presidential adviser to Paz [@roguero_2026_cerimedo]. An Argentine political consultant known for his use of bot farms, Cerimedo had been involved with several of Latin America's new wave of far-right leaders (Milei in Argentina, Kast in Chile, Bolsonaro in Brazil, and Asfura in Honduras). His former girlfriend began publicly releasing photographs and private communications, exposing the extent of his role and revealing that he had played a significantly larger part in Paz's government than had been publicly acknowledged. Vice-president Lara added further pressure by asserting that Cerimedo had exercised real power and taken decisions within the Paz administration, and published unverified audio recordings attributed to conversations involving Cerimedo and members of Paz's inner circle, including his wife. Beller also claimed to hold evidence of alleged irregular business dealings involving Paz and his family [@lissardy_2026_cerimedo].

In September 2026, the US Department of State designated Bolivia's Attorney General Roger Mariaca for his alleged “involvement in significant corruption”, making Mariaca and his immediate family members generally ineligible for entry into the United States [@state_department_2026_visa_restrictions]. Three days after the designation, Mariaca was arrested over alleged links to Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset, who was extradited to the United States in March 2026 [@eldeber_2026_irusta_aprehension]. The Public Prosecutor's office denounced the arrest as illegal [@dw_2026_bolivia_mariaca], while some observers have linked the arrest of Mariaca to his investigation into the activities of Cerimedo.

In July 2026, Bolivia reached a \$1.9 billion staff-level agreement with the IMF, although the agreement still requires approval from the IMF’s Executive Board and Bolivia's Congress. If approved, the deal would mark Bolivia's first multi-year IMF arrangement since 2006 and the reforms associated with the programme are likely to have significant structural consequences and could generate further social unrest.

### Brazil

The election of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2002 brought the Workers’ Party (PT) to power. A former metalworker and trade-union leader, Lula was re-elected in 2006 and served until 2010. His governments combined macroeconomic stability with social policies, notably *Bolsa Família*, a cash-transfer programme for low-income families conditional on school attendance and health check-ups, alongside minimum-wage increases and measures to reduce poverty and inequality. Economic growth benefited from the commodities boom and rising Chinese demand for Brazilian exports. Lula’s administration also sought to strengthen Brazil’s international standing through South–South cooperation, multilateral diplomacy and the BRICS grouping. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, had served as minister of mines and energy and subsequently as Lula’s chief of staff. Elected in 2010 and re-elected in 2014, she continued the PT’s social and economic agenda but faced recession, mounting political opposition and the Lava Jato (Car Wash) investigation into corruption at the state oil company Petrobras, which implicated politicians across the governing coalition [@crs_brazil_background_2016]. Rousseff now heads the BRICS-founded New Development Bank (NDB).

Rousseff was removed from office in August 2016 following an impeachment trial in the Senate, which convicted her of violating fiscal and budgetary rules. However, the proceedings were deeply entangled with political manoeuvring. In December 2015, Eduardo Cunha, then president of the Chamber of Deputies and himself facing an ethics investigation over alleged corruption linked to Petrobras, reportedly threatened to accept the impeachment petition unless PT lawmakers on the Chamber’s ethics committee voted against investigating him. Rousseff’s removal also reflected the collapse of her political support amid a severe recession, with GDP contracting by more than 3% in both 2015 and 2016, unemployment reaching 11% and rising inflation. Mass street protests, hostile press coverage and growing isolation in Congress further weakened her position. Secret recordings published in May 2016 also showed Romero Jucá, a senior senator and ally of Rousseff’s vice-president, Michel Temer, appearing to link her removal to halting the Lava Jato investigation. Critics further interpreted the financial markets’ positive reaction to the progress of impeachment as evidence of business and financial circles’ preference for a change of government. Rousseff denounced her impeachment as a parliamentary coup, while her opponents maintained that the fiscal violations warranted her dismissal. Although the process followed constitutional procedures, its political legitimacy remained contested. Temer, from the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB, now MDB), succeeded her and pursued a more market-oriented agenda, including spending restraints and labour-market reform [@elpais_dilma_impeachment_2016; @guardian_dilma_impeachment_2016].

The political crisis also exposed the increasingly contentious relationship between electoral competition, anti-corruption investigations and the judiciary. In the 2018 presidential election, the PT initially nominated former President Lula da Silva, who was the clear favourite in the polls. However, the party was forced to replace him at the last minute with Fernando Haddad, a former mayor of São Paulo, after the electoral court barred Lula, who was in prison following a corruption conviction that was later annulled. Lula spent 580 days in prison, while Haddad, hindered by a late start and his low national profile, eventually lost the runoff to Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain who campaigned on an anti-establishment, socially conservative and strongly anti-PT platform.

In 2021, the Supreme Federal Court annulled Lula’s convictions on jurisdictional grounds, ruling that the cases should not have been tried by the court in Curitiba, which restored his political rights. In a separate decision, a panel of the Court found that former judge Sérgio Moro had acted with bias in the proceedings against Lula. These judgments undermined the validity of the convictions and reinforced concerns about the political contamination of the anti-corruption campaign [@folha_lula_convictions_2021; @guardian_lula_bias_2021; @intercept_moro_dallagnol_chats_2019].

Bolsonaro’s presidency, from 2019 to 2022, marked a sharp ideological shift. His administration promoted pension reform, privatisation and a reduced role for the state in the economy, while advancing socially conservative positions. Environmental protection weakened, and deforestation in the Amazon increased. Bolsonaro also defended Brazil’s military dictatorship and repeatedly challenged democratic institutions, particularly the electoral system. In foreign policy, he cultivated a close ideological relationship with Donald Trump during the latter’s first presidency. Yet this alignment had important limits. Bolsonaro’s rhetoric could be hostile towards Beijing, but China remained indispensable to Brazil’s export economy, particularly for soybeans, beef and iron ore. The contradiction between political affinity with Washington and economic dependence on China exposed a structural constraint on any attempt to reorient Brazilian foreign policy too sharply towards the United States [@guardian_bolsonaro_amazon_2019; @guardian_bolsonaro_elected_2018; @debolle_2026_lula_bolsonaro].

Lula returned to the presidency in January 2023 after defeating Bolsonaro in the October 2022 election. Bolsonaro refused to accept the result, and on 8 January 2023 his supporters stormed the presidential palace, Congress and Supreme Court buildings in Brasília in an attempt to create conditions for overturning Lula’s victory. In September 2025, Bolsonaro was convicted by the Supreme Federal Court of organising a coup and attempting to violently abolish democracy, among other crimes, and sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison. He was subsequently placed under house arrest for medical reasons [@brito_bolsonaro_coup_sentence_2025].

Lula’s third presidency sought to revive social redistribution, strengthen domestic industry and restore Brazil’s international profile. His government has pursued closer diplomatic and economic relations with China, Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. Beijing has also expanded its presence in sectors such as electric vehicles, renewable energy, telecommunications and industrial technology. This partnership offers Brazil significant markets and investment, but also creates tensions with Lula’s objective of reindustrialising the economy and developing domestic technological capacity. Chinese companies are increasingly competing with Brazilian producers, while Brazil’s reliance on commodity exports makes it vulnerable to changes in Chinese demand [@debolle_2026_lula_bolsonaro].

Relations between Lula’s government and the Trump administration have remained pragmatic but fraught with tensions. In July 2025, Washington announced tariffs reaching 50% on many Brazilian imports, linking the measures in part to the prosecution of Bolsonaro. The United States also sanctioned Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who had played a prominent role in proceedings against the former president. Lula rejected the pressure as interference in Brazil’s sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary.

In 2026, the dispute extended into the presidential campaign. The Trump administration designated Brazil’s two dominant criminal organisations, the *Primeiro Comando da Capital* (PCC) and *Comando Vermelho*, as terrorist organisations. The designations, announced in the middle of the campaign, politicised the issue of public security, and their timing raised questions about Washington’s motives, given that the United States had not previously treated these groups as such a threat. There is also no evidence that *Comando Vermelho* had a significant presence in the United States or was substantially involved in its financial system. The trafficking routes dominated by these groups and the markets in which they operated were primarily oriented towards Europe rather than the United States [@dudley_newton_2026_brazil_elections]. Flávio Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s son and Lula’s principal challenger in the 2026 election, used the issue to accuse the incumbent of being weak on crime [@elpais_trump_brazil_tariffs_2025; @phillips_2026_brazil; @guardian_trump_brazil_interference_2026].

A related controversy concerned the influence of American technology companies over Brazil’s democratic process. During the 2026 campaign, Lula and his allies accused Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro. According to reports based on internal communications, Meta employees acknowledged that restrictions had hindered Lula’s Instagram accounts during the election [@teles_meta_lula_accounts_2026].

The presidential runoff on 25 October 2026 provided a further test of Brazil’s political polarisation and its international orientation. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.79% of valid votes against 48.21%, becoming the first candidate since the restoration of direct presidential elections in 1989 to win a runoff after finishing second in the first round. Lula’s campaign overhauled his social media strategy, while his government introduced a series of popular economic and social measures in the run-up to the election. These included a 15% increase in *Bolsa Família* payments, a new household debt-renegotiation programme, and a constitutional amendment reducing the maximum working week from 44 to 40 hours without cutting pay. His victory secured a fourth term and represented a setback for Trump’s efforts to strengthen the position of ideologically aligned governments across Latin America. Flávio initially rejected the result and called for the election to be annulled, echoing his father’s refusal to accept defeat in 2022. Just two days after his defeat he left Brazil for the United States amid an investigation into alleged money laundering [@elpais_lula_election_win_2026; @elpais_bolsonaro_argentina_escape_2026].

Trump openly criticised the Brazilian election, telling reporters that it “looked terrible” and resembled “another rigged election”. He also said he would be willing to receive Flávio Bolsonaro and his family in the United States after their departure from Brazil [@ionova_ellick_nicas_lula_social_media_2026; @elpais_bolsonaro_argentina_escape_2026]. In his victory speech, Lula rejected US ambitions in the Western Hemisphere and declared that Brazil would not be “anyone’s backyard”. He also rejected placing Brazil within a bipolar framework dominated by rivalry between the United States and China, emphasising the country’s determination to pursue an autonomous path. This ambition extends to technology, with Lula declaring, “I do not want to remain dependent on Chinese or American artificial intelligence; I want to create a Brazilian one” [@legrandcontinent_lula_victory_2026]. Lula’s fourth term will thus begin with a clear diplomatic orientation but difficult domestic constraints, as he faces a hostile Congress, persistent economic pressures, demands for improved public security and continuing disputes over the legitimacy of public institutions [@guardian_lula_victory_2026].

### Chile

Chile’s recent political trajectory has been marked by persistent anti-incumbency. The last time a president handed power to a successor from the same political camp was in 2006, when Ricardo Lagos of the centre-left Concertación was succeeded by fellow coalition member Michelle Bachelet. Every presidential election since has resulted in a change of political camp: Sebastián Piñera’s centre-right government replaced Bachelet’s in 2010, she returned to office in 2014, Piñera won again in 2018, and left-wing Gabriel Boric defeated him in 2021 before losing to right-wing José Antonio Kast in 2025. This recurring rejection of the governing camp reflects widespread disenchantment with political parties and distrust in institutions, alongside shifting concerns over inequality, security, migration and economic performance [@rivas_molina_2025_pendulo_chile].

The mass protests of 2019, driven by grievances over inequality and the cost of living, prompted a process to replace the Constitution inherited from the Pinochet dictatorship. In the October 2020 referendum, 78 per cent voted to begin drafting a new constitution. Boric, a left-wing candidate who drew support from the protest movement, defeated Kast in the 2021 presidential election. However, the draft produced by a predominantly left-wing constitutional convention was rejected by 62 per cent of voters in September 2022. A second proposal, drawn up by a conservative-dominated body, was also rejected in December 2023, this time by 56 per cent. The rejection of both proposals underscored the diffulty of building a consensus on constitutional change and left the country's underlying political divisions unresolved. Against a backdrop of continuing concerns about crime, migration and economic performance, Kast defeated the governing coalition’s candidate, Jeannette Jara, with 58 per cent of the vote in December 2025. His victory continued the pattern of incumbent defeat while also fitting the broader rightward shift seen across Latin America [@montes_2020_chile_constitution_plebiscite; @rivas_molina_montes_2021_boric_election; @rivas_molina_montes_2022_rejected_constitution; @montes_2023_rejected_right_constitution; @villegas_cambero_2025_kast_election]

The closer alignment between Washington and Santiago under Kast contrasts with some of the discrepancies that characterised relations under the Boric administration. In February 2026, shortly before Kast took office, the Trump administration revoked the visas of three Chilean officials involved in the assessment of a proposed undersea fibre-optic cable linking Chile to Hong Kong, arguing that the project compromised critical telecommunications infrastructure and regional security. US Ambassador to Chile Brandon Judd defended the measure, saying that visa sanctions “were not meant to punish, but to change behaviour” [@rodriguez_mega_2026_visa]. The episode illustrates the extent to which the Trump administration has used visa restrictions as an instrument of foreign-policy pressure in the region, particularly in relation to China's growing presence in Latin America.

Under Kast, Chile has subsequently moved closer to Washington. In September 2026, his government joined Trump's “Shield of the Americas”, a regional initiative presented by Washington as a framework for cooperation on security but which also encompasses economic and multilateral coordination. The initiative has provoked a significant political debate in Chile. Former presidents Michelle Bachelet and Gabriel Boric jointly called on the Kast government to reconsider Chile's participation, arguing that Chile should not be forced to choose sides in the current geopolitical context [@sanhueza_2026_kast_escudo_americas].

Kast's foreign-policy orientation also reflects his ideological proximity to other right-wing governments in the region. On 3 September 2026, Santiago hosted the fifth regional meeting of the Madrid Forum, which presents itself as a network of American and European right-wing forces and has become an important meeting place for the right in Latin America. Argentine President Javier Milei was one of the event's main speakers. In his speech, Milei referred to the overthrow of Salvador Allende, Chile's democratically elected socialist president, as the beginning of a period of stability and economic growth under Augusto Pinochet, arguing that Chile subsequently became the envy of the region economically [@forti_2026_milei]. His remarks drew criticism in Chile not only from the opposition but also from within Kast's governing coalition. While Kast's Republican Party endorsed Milei's comments, they were rejected by the centre-right Independent Democratic Union (UDI) [@forti_2026_milei].

Kast’s presidency represents both a significant shift in Chile’s political orientation and the continuation of its long-standing pattern of anti-incumbency. His early decline in popularity has exposed the gap between his campaign promises and the difficulties of governing. By October 2026, his approval rating had fallen to 27 per cent, while 64 per cent disapproved of his performance and 82 per cent said the government had fallen short of their expectations. The decline has extended beyond opposition voters to include people who voted for Kast and other right-wing voters. Having campaigned on an “emergency government” that would quickly revive the economy and impose tougher controls on crime and irregular migration, he has yet to deliver the improvements voters expected. Fiscal adjustments, including cuts affecting health, education, science, culture and social programmes, have added to dissatisfaction amid rising living costs and economic stagnation. His government has also struggled to secure legislative agreements, while ministerial missteps have weakened confidence in its competence [@dannemann_2026_kast_popularity_decline; @andrade_2026_kast_criteria_approval]. If this trend continues, Kast could become the latest president whose political camp is rejected at the next election.

### Colombia

Colombian politics since 2000 has been dominated by right and centre-right governments with the election of Gustavo Petro in 2022 marking a historic break with this pattern. Álvaro Uribe, elected president in 2002 and re-elected in 2006, built a powerful right-wing political movement around a hard-line security agenda and deep hostility towards the guerrillas, in particular the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). His two governments were closely aligned with Washington during the Bush era, and implemented market-friendly economic policies.

His successor, Juan Manuel Santos, had served as Uribe’s defence minister, initially seen as his continuity candidate, subsequently broke with him over negotiations with the FARC. He negotiated and signed the 2016 peace agreement with FARC, gaining the Nobel Peace Prize for it, but the agreement was ultimately rejected by voters in a referendum (50.2% against, 49.8% in favour) though a renegotiated version was subsequently ratified by Congress.

Iván Duque, elected in 2018 with Uribe’s support, represented a return to a more confrontational approach to the peace process. The election of Petro, a former M-19 guerrilla and leader of the left-wing Historic Pact coalition, therefore marks a a watershed moment for Colombia as he became its first left-wing president, partly due to widespread discontent with inequality, social exclusion and the established political elite [@canelas_2022_uribismo_decline; @parkin_daniels_bolanos_2022_petro_first_leftist].

Petro pledged sweeping social transformation, but his reform agenda was repeatedly slowed or blocked by a fragmented Congress, judicial scrutiny and institutional resistance. His flagship *Paz Total* policy, aimed at negotiating with armed groups, produced limited progress, while violence and the territorial influence of illegal armed actors remained serious concerns. In October 2025, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Petro, his wife, his son and a close associate, accusing them of allegedly permitting drug cartels to operate with impunity [@us_treasury_2025_petro_sanctions].

The 2026 presidential election brought a striking change in political direction with the victory of Abelardo De La Espriella, who defeated left-wing candidate Iván Cepeda in the June run-off. De La Espriella is a wealthy criminal defence lawyer who had never held elected office and presented himself as an anti-establishment outsider. His rise is part of a broader regional trend towards personalist, hard-right political movements, but it was not simply a return to the traditional Colombian right. He rejected the established parties and portrayed himself as a political outsider, while advocating a security-first agenda inspired by Nayib Bukele in El Salvador and a radical reduction in the size of the state modelled on Javier Milei in Argentina. His outsider image was nevertheless complicated by the public endorsement he received from former president Álvaro Uribe after the first round. De La Espriella also received Donald Trump’s endorsement ahead of the run-off, which he presented as an opportunity to reset relations with Washington [@correal2026_colombia_trump_endorsement; @martin_2026_de_la_espriella_outsider; @reuters_2026_trump_endorsement].

De La Espriella’s programme combines an aggressive security agenda with market-oriented economic policies. He promised to end negotiations with armed groups, build ten mega-prisons, resume aerial eradication of coca crops, expand oil and gas exploration and abolish the wealth tax. He also pledged to reduce the size of the state by as much as 40 per cent [@stacey_2026_de_la_espriella_program; @epoch_times_2026_espriella_speech]. On taking office on 7 August 2026, he announced that Colombia would join Trump’s *Shield of the Americas*, a regional security initiative focused on organised crime and drug trafficking. He delivered his inaugural address at the Pichincha Battalion in Cali directly to military and police commanders, reinforcing the centrality of security to his administration’s agenda.

There is, however, a contradiction between De La Espriella’s promise of radical austerity, his criticism towards Petro for overspending and his own government’s first budget proposal. The draft 2027 budget submitted to Congress was 10 per cent larger than the proposal presented by Petro’s administration [@quintero_2026_de_la_espriella_budget; @freixes_2026_spending]. De La Espriella also built a reputation in Miami representing high-profile Colombian clients, many of them charged with drug trafficking and corruption or linked to right-wing paramilitaries, the kind of clientele he now vows to pursue as president.

The foreign-policy shift has been most visible in relations with the United States. De La Espriella spent almost a decade in Miami and became a naturalised US citizen in 2023, while cultivating ties with Republican politicians. His relationship with Washington predates his presidency as he had donated to the campaigns of Florida Republican congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, who also publicly supported his presidential bid. Trump’s endorsement during the Colombian campaign and the new government’s decision to join the *Shield of the Americas* have since been followed by a closer security partnership. On 7 August, the US administration announced plans to provide Colombia with a \$1 billion security assistance package, signalling closer alignment in bilateral relations after the repeated confrontations between Trump and Petro [@stacey_2026_de_la_espriella_us_ties; @usdos2026_colombia]. The shift in bilateral relations extends to Colombia’s position on the International Criminal Court. Colombia has been a party to the Rome Statute since November 2002. In May 2026, shortly before the transfer of power, the ICC Office of the Prosecutor and Colombian authorities reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation and complementarity, building on the agreement signed in 2021 [@icc_2026_colombia_cooperation]. Since De La Espriella took office, however, his government has signalled a markedly different approach. It withdrew Colombia’s candidate for an ICC judgeship, while the president’s administration has advocated the possibility of withdrawing from the Rome Statute. The shift has unfolded amid explicit US pressure as Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of war, urged countries participating in the *Shield of the Americas* to leave the ICC, while Washington has pursued a broader campaign against the Court [@parada_lugo_2026_colombia_icc_candidate; @garces_2026_icc_us_pressure].

A related change concerns Colombia’s position before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), not to be confused with the ICC. Under Petro, Colombia had intervened in South Africa’s case against Israel under the Genocide Convention, in which South Africa alleges that Israel’s conduct in Gaza violates the Convention. On 22 September 2026, the De La Espriella government formally withdrew Colombia’s declaration of intervention in that case [@colombia_mfa_2026_icj_withdrawal]. This was part of a broader realignment with Israel and a departure from Petro’s approach to the Gaza war.

Petro had broken diplomatic relations with Israel in 2024 and halted Colombian coal exports to the country in protest against its military campaign in Gaza. De La Espriella reversed this policy, restored diplomatic relations and recognised Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, making Colombia only the second country in the world, after the United States, to officially recognise Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, breaking with the prevailing international position that the territory remains Syrian. On 14 October 2026, Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem and restored its free-trade agreement with Israel, reversing another element of the previous government’s policy [@pita_2026_colombia_golan_recognition; @reuters_2026_colombia_embassy_jerusalem].

The alignment with the United States and Israel was highly visible during the response to the devastating earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August, three days after De La Espriella took office. Although several countries offered assistance, the foreign search-and-rescue teams initially admitted by Bogotá came from the United States, Israel, Ecuador and El Salvador, while teams offered by countries including Mexico and Brazil were not initially accepted. The selective admission of search-and-rescue teams offered a striking early illustration of the new government’s foreign-policy priorities.

### Costa Rica

The February 2026 presidential and legislative elections marked an important continuation of the political shift initiated by Rodrigo Chaves, who had been president since 2022 but was constitutionally barred from seeking a second consecutive term. Chaves nevertheless remained the dominant figure behind the newly created *Partido Pueblo Soberano* (PPSO), and his former Minister of Planning, Laura Fernández Delgado, was chosen as its presidential candidate. Fernández won 48.5% of the vote in the first round, comfortably exceeding the 40% threshold required for an outright victory, making Costa Rica one of the relatively few cases in the region in recent years in which the governing political movement successfully retained the presidency [@eu_eem_2026_costa_rica]. PPSO also won 31 of the 57 seats in the Legislative Assembly, giving Fernández an absolute majority and the largest parliamentary bloc since 1982. The new government is therefore in a significantly stronger position to pass ordinary legislation and the national budget without having to negotiate with other parties [@eu_eem_2026_costa_rica].

Fernández's candidacy was explicitly presented as a continuation of Chaves's political project. During his presidency, Chaves adopted an increasingly confrontational stance towards other branches of government and oversight institutions, repeatedly accusing the Legislative Assembly, the judiciary, the Prosecutor General's Office, the Comptroller's Office and, most notably, the Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) of obstructing his government's policies. This rhetoric contributed to declining confidence in public institutions, particularly among PPSO supporters [@eu_eem_2026_costa_rica]. Fernández has also pledged to continue Chaves's hard-line approach to security as Costa Rica faces a severe deterioration in public safety, including record levels of homicide and drug-related violence. Chaves himself has remained directly involved in government, having been appointed Minister of the Presidency and Minister of Finance in Fernández's administration, giving him a central role in coordinating the new government's political and economic agenda.

Foreign policy has likewise remained closely aligned with the United States. Costa Rica has long cooperated with Washington on counternarcotics and maritime security, but this relationship deepened under Chaves and has continued under Fernández. In March 2026, Costa Rica joined the Trump administration's “Shield of the Americas” initiative against drug trafficking and organised crime. It also agreed to accept up to 25 migrants deported from the United States each week from third countries, making Costa Rica part of the Trump administration's broader effort to transfer deportees to countries other than their countries of origin [@crs_2026_costa_rica].

Costa Rica nevertheless maintains significant economic ties with China. The two countries established diplomatic relations in 2007, and China has since become an important economic partner, including through a free-trade agreement, infrastructure financing and investment. Under Chaves, however, relations became more contentious, particularly over telecommunications. In 2023, Costa Rica excluded companies from countries that had not ratified the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime from participating in the development of its 5G network, effectively preventing Chinese companies such as Huawei from bidding. The decision was welcomed by Washington but criticised by Beijing and became part of a broader dispute over Chinese involvement in Costa Rica's strategic infrastructure [@crs_2026_costa_rica].

Costa Rica's foreign-policy orientation therefore combines close strategic and security cooperation with Washington with continued economic relations with China. This places Costa Rica within the broader regional trend towards closer alignment with Washington, while illustrating that such alignment does not necessarily extend to disengagement from China economically.

An additional important development in Costa Rica's international profile is its candidacy for the next United Nations Secretary-General. In March 2026, the government formally nominated former Vice-President and former UNCTAD (UN Trade and Development) Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis for the position for the 2027–2031 term [@costa_rica_2026_grynspan_unsg]. The new Fernández government subsequently reaffirmed its support for her candidacy. By September, Grynspan had emerged as the narrow frontrunner in several informal UN Security Council straw polls, although the selection process remains open. Her candidacy also reflects Costa Rica's continuing emphasis on multilateral diplomacy alongside its increasingly close security relationship with Washington.

### Cuba

Since the beginning of 2026, Washington has imposed an oil blockade on Havana alongside intensified economic sanctions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants who has made toppling Cuba's communist government a personal project, described the measures as “the strongest sanctions in the history” of bilateral relations [@colome_2026_cuba_us_strategy]. Heavily reliant on imported oil, Cuba previously received most of its supplies from Venezuela. Those shipments stopped after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, and no Venezuelan oil has reached the island since. The resulting energy shortage has plunged Cuba into repeated nationwide blackouts. With the exception of the Russian tanker *Anatoly Kolodkin*, which delivered oil to Cuba in March, no significant alternative supplies have reached the island. Even countries sympathetic to Cuba, including Mexico and Brazil, have been reluctant to ship fuel because of the risk of retaliation and sanctions from Washington. The US administration has explicitly threatened tariffs against countries that provide oil to Cuba [@colome_2026_cuba_us_strategy].

The effects have extended beyond energy. Shipping containers carrying food, medicine and other goods bound for Cuba have been stranded throughout the Caribbean after the main shipping companies stopped serving the island for fear of sanctions. According to the Cuban ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva, more than 7,000 containers have been affected. The lack of medicine and rising food prices have created what has been described as the most severe humanitarian crisis on the island since the 1959 revolution [@augustin_robles_2026_cuba_sanctions].

In September 2026, the US Coast Guard intercepted the *Grace*, a vessel that US authorities said was carrying fuel to Cuba, in violation of international law \[\@adams_2026_cuba_fuel_ships\]. Cuban Foreign Minister, Bruno Rodríguez, denounced the US blockade at the United Nations General Assembly as an act of war [@adams_2026_cuba_fuel_ships]. Cuba is producing some fuel domestically, but nowhere near enough to meet its needs. At the same time, the limited oil that does reach the island is increasingly being imported by private businesses from the United States. As a result, US exports to Cuba have risen sharply: from just over \$416.5 million in 2025 to almost \$700 million in 2026, an increase of around 61% [@colome_2026_cuba_us_strategy].

The political objective of the policy is explicit. President Donald Trump stated at the United Nations General Assembly that his administration was “seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba” [@trump2026_unga81]. The combination of cutting off Cuba's traditional sources of fuel, deterring third countries from supplying the island and allowing selected private-sector imports from the United States is placing severe pressure on the Cuban economy while increasing the role of US-linked private commerce.

As a result of the economic crisis, Cuba has experienced the largest outflow of people in its history since 2020. Estimates range from 13% of the population according to official figures to as much as 25% according to independent estimates, representing approximately 1.6 to 2.75 million people [@cfr_cuba_mass_exodus]. What began as a response to Cuba's post-pandemic economic collapse has evolved into a crisis of its own, as public services are increasingly affected by the loss of personnel, from teachers and nurses to doctors. Initially, the United States continued to offer relatively generous pathways to legal residency to newly arrived Cubans, but this changed under the second Trump administration, which ultimately redirected migration flows. Hundreds of thousands of Cubans applied for Spanish citizenship, while many thousands more travelled to countries such as Brazil and Uruguay [@cfr_cuba_mass_exodus].

During the first half of 2026, a US military intervention in Cuba appeared increasingly possible. Subsequent backchannel talks between Havana and Washington offered a potential way out of the crisis, reportedly involving the removal of President Miguel Díaz-Canel. The policy now appears to have shifted, however, with Secretary of State Rubio stating that the Cuban regime could survive into 2028 and beyond [@freeman_2026_cuba_point_no_return]. One possibility is that Washington is deliberately maintaining economic pressure to strengthen its position in future negotiations or to further weaken the Cuban military in preparation for a possible intervention. Another is that, with the United States preoccupied with Iran and managing the situation in Venezuela, Cuba has simply become a less immediate priority.

### Ecuador

Daniel Roy Gilchrist Noboa Azín has been president of Ecuador since November 2023, when, at the age of 35, he became the country's youngest elected president. He was re-elected in 2025 for a full four-year term. Noboa holds dual US and Ecuadorian citizenship and is the son of Álvaro Noboa, one of Ecuador's wealthiest businessmen. He has pursued a strongly militarised approach to combating organised crime, declaring an “internal armed conflict” against criminal groups in January 2024. The strategy has had limited success, however, with the homicide rate increasing sharply from 2022 onwards after a decade of comparatively low levels [@statista_2026_ecuador_homicide]. The militarisation of public security has also generated serious human-rights concerns. Amnesty International has documented the enforced disappearance of ten people in the context of military security operations, including six children [@amnesty_2026_ecuador_militarization].

Noboa has simultaneously moved Ecuador closer to the United States, particularly in the fight against drug trafficking and organised crime. Ecuador was among the initial participants in Trump's “Shield of the Americas”, a regional initiative centred on security cooperation and the fight against drug trafficking. In September 2026, the US designated Ecuador's Los Tiguerones gang as a terrorist organisation [@theguardian_2026_ecuador_tiguerones]. Noboa's dual US-Ecuadorian citizenship and his close security relationship with Washington are also consistent with his broader orientation towards the United States, although his foreign policy has not amounted to a complete geopolitical realignment.

Ecuador remains deeply economically dependent on China, which has financed major infrastructure projects, including the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, and is the country's largest buyer of shrimp. In February 2026, Noboa travelled to China to meet with Chinese leaders, a move that risked causing concern in Washington. He subsequently stressed that, while the United States was an important partner in security and the fight against organised crime, Ecuador could not neglect its economic relations with countries such as China and Russia [@canizares2026_noboa_china].

Ecuador therefore illustrates the broader regional trend towards closer security cooperation with Washington while also demonstrating the limits of such alignment. Noboa has embraced the Trump administration's regional security agenda and strengthened Ecuador's ties with the United States, while maintaining significant economic interdependence with China.

### El Salvador

Nayib Bukele became president at the age of 37 in 2019 and was re-elected by a landslide in 2024 [@kitroeff_2024_bukele_election]. His presidency has been dominated by his campaign against gang violence, which has made him one of Latin America's most popular leaders, but also by the concentration of political power and the erosion of civil liberties.

His government gained a legislative supermajority in 2021, allowing Bukele and his *Nuevas Ideas* party to exert increasing control over the legislature, judiciary and other state institutions. The Supreme Court, whose judges had been appointed by the legislature after Bukele's party removed the previous magistrates, ruled in 2021 that he could seek a second consecutive term, despite the previous constitutional prohibition [@bbc_2021_el_salvador_reelection_bukele]. In 2025, the legislature subsequently abolished presidential term limits, allowing Bukele to seek indefinite re-election.

The turning point of the security crackdown came in March 2022, when a surge in gang violence prompted the government to declare a state of emergency that has remained in force ever since. The measure greatly expanded the powers of the police and armed forces and enabled mass arrests [@abi_habib_2022_el_salvador_arrests]. More than 90,000 people have since been detained, bringing the prison population to approximately 120,000 and giving El Salvador one of the world's highest incarceration rates [@wagner_2026_el_salvador_mass_trials]. The government subsequently introduced tougher penalties for gang membership, removed limits on pretrial detention and authorised mass trials in which up to 900 defendants can be prosecuted together when allegedly linked to the same criminal organisation [@wagner_2026_el_salvador_mass_trials]. Human rights organisations have documented widespread due-process violations and cases of people being detained without credible evidence. In late 2024, Bukele acknowledged that 8,000 people detained during the crackdown had subsequently been released because they were innocent [@swissinfo_2024_bukele_innocents]. Human rights groups have said that this number is much higher and estimate that roughly 30,000 innocent people were arrested [@wagner_2026_el_salvador_mass_trials].

The crackdown has nevertheless produced a dramatic decline in violent crime, transforming El Salvador from one of the world's most dangerous countries into one of the safest. El Salvador's homicide rate, which stood at 103 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2015, fell steadily over the following decade to 1.3 in 2025 [@statista_2026_el_salvador_homicide]. The government's security policies have enjoyed substantial domestic support, despite continuing criticism over their human-rights consequences.

More than four years after the mass arrests began, detainees are now being brought to trial in large groups. Human Rights Watch has documented serious deficiencies in these proceedings, including restrictions on the right to defence, violations of international human rights standards and the near-universal conviction of defendants in mass trials [@hrw_2026_el_salvador_mass_trials].

In terms of foreign policy, under former Salvadoran president Salvador Sánchez Cerén (2014–2019), El Salvador broke off relations with Taiwan in 2018 and recognised the People’s Republic of China. One of Beijing’s gifts to the country in exchange for its support was the US\$54 million National Library in the historic centre of San Salvador. Inaugurated in November 2023, the modern building was promoted by Bukele as a legacy for future generations, as well as a symbol of his government’s achievements [@vigna_2024_el_salvador_china_library].

Bukele has also developed a particularly close relationship with the United States under Donald Trump. In February 2025, he offered to accept people deported from the United States, including alleged criminals from third countries, for detention in Salvadoran prisons in return for a fee. In March 2025, the United States transferred 238 Venezuelans alleged to be members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang to El Salvador's CECOT prison, paying the Salvadoran government \$6 million for one year of detention [@reuters_2025_el_salvador_tren_de_aragua]. The arrangement has made El Salvador an important partner in the Trump administration's efforts to expand deportations and externalise immigration detention, while also giving Bukele a prominent role in Washington's regional security agenda.

### Guatemala

The political climate in Guatemala is characterised by deep polarisation, the instrumentalisation of the judicial system for political purposes, and the penetration of criminal organisations and sophisticated corruption networks into state institutions [@eu_efm_2025_guatemala]. The country saw a significant political change with the election of Bernardo Arévalo in 2023 and his inauguration in January 2024. His election was followed by months of political uncertainty, as opponents sought to challenge the result through legal and procedural means. The Attorney General's Office and other judicial actors pursued cases against members of Arévalo's *Semilla Movement*, the political party that brought him to power, whose legal status was definitively cancelled in March 2026. Arévalo's victory was initially greeted with considerable optimism, but enthusiasm has since been tempered by frustration among some of his supporters, who had expected more rapid and far-reaching change [@freeman2026_guatemala_democracy]. Arévalo's ability to implement his agenda is constrained by his lack of a majority in Congress and by the broader fragmentation of the political system. He has deliberately sought to pursue reform within the existing constitutional and legal framework rather than confront entrenched interests through extra-legal means. This approach reflects his commitment to democratic and constitutional procedures, but has also fuelled a debate among reformers over whether such caution is sufficient to dismantle deeply entrenched networks of corruption and political influence [@freeman2026_guatemala_democracy].

Arévalo's administration has nevertheless made progress in some areas of public service provision and institutional reform. The government has expanded recruitment in education and reported improvements in school infrastructure and healthcare provision. However, major legislative initiatives on corruption and judicial reform have been stalled or blocked in a fragmented Congress in which Arévalo lacks a majority.

Cooperation with the United States on counternarcotics and organised crime provides a channel for continued communication and interaction between the two administrations, but does not imply close political alignment. Arévalo's opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers [@freeman2026_guatemala_democracy]. In March 2026, it was revealed that US embassy staff, including the US ambassador to Guatemala, had called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a controversial Constitutional Court judge whose past associations with drug traffickers and gang members had raised concerns [@freeman2026_guatemala_democracy; @france24_2026_guatemala_magistrado]. The revelations prompted President Arévalo's administration to seek explanations from the US State Department [@menchu2026_arevalo_magistrados]. Ultimately, with the appointment of the contested candidate, Roberto Molina Barreto, the Court is tied between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority on the Court.

Guatemala's next general elections are scheduled for 2027. Arévalo is constitutionally barred from seeking a second term, and no unifying candidate has yet emerged from his political camp capable of continuing and consolidating his reforms, raising the risk that they could be reversed under a new government.

### Guyana

<https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/19/world/americas/guyana-oil-boom.html>

### Haiti

Haiti's last presidential election was held in October 2015. The country is now preparing for elections scheduled for 13 December 2026, but severe logistical and security challenges have raised doubts about whether they can take place as planned, with many experts expecting a postponement [@paultre_robles_2026_haiti_election]. Haiti has been under pressure from the international community, including the United States, to restore an elected government. However, insecurity has displaced large numbers of voters and prevented many from returning to their communities to cast their ballots, while kidnappings and killings remain pervasive. This has created a fundamental dilemma: while some argue that elections cannot be held without first restoring security, others see an elected government as a prerequisite for restoring legitimate state authority and security.

Haiti last elected a president in 2016, when Jovenel Moïse came to power. He was assassinated in July 2021, after which gang violence, already a persistent feature of Haitian politics and society, escalated further, culminating in a major surge in violence in early 2024 [@paultre_robles_2026_haiti_election]. Armed groups still control large parts of Port-au-Prince and have expanded their presence beyond the capital. The Kenya-led Multinational Security Support Mission began deploying in June 2024, with the aim of supporting the Haitian national police and creating conditions for elections, but suffered from severe funding and personnel shortages and never reached its planned strength of 2,500 personnel. In September 2025, it was replaced by the UN-authorised Gang Suppression Force, with a planned strength of 5,500 personnel but only around 1,500 had been deployed by September 2026 [@unsoh_2026_background]. With elections already six years overdue, pressure to hold them is considerable, but the continuing security crisis raises doubts about whether they can take place as planned and whether voters across the country will be able to participate.

### Honduras

Honduras was governed by the conservative *Partido Nacional* for twelve consecutive years, from 2010 to 2022, first under Porfirio Lobo and then under Juan Orlando Hernández (JOH), with the sole interruption being the presidency of Xiomara Castro (2022–2026), wife of Manuel Zelaya, who was ousted in a coup in 2009. The victory of Nasry “Tito” Asfura in the November 2025 elections therefore represented a return to power for the party that had dominated Honduran politics for much of the preceding decade. His victory was exceptionally narrow, with a margin of roughly 27,000 votes [@eu_eom_2026_honduras], and remains contested as the runner-up, Salvador Nasralla, refuses to recognise the result and alleges electoral fraud. One development that has intensified the allegations is the publication in August 2026 of audio recordings by a former member of the electoral tribunal, Marlon Ochoa, in which Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo, who advised the *Partido Nacional* campaign, is heard stating that votes were introduced in favour of Asfura in certain ballot boxes and that votes unfavourable to the candidate were removed [@duarte2026_cerimedo_honduras].

Asfura's victory was also closely associated with Donald Trump, who openly intervened in the campaign days before the election, endorsing Asfura and warning that US support could be reconsidered if he lost [@wagner2025_honduras_trump]. Two days before the election, Trump also announced a full pardon for Juan Orlando Hernández [@correal2025_honduras_hernandez_pardon], the former president convicted in 2024 by a US federal court of conspiring to import cocaine into the United States and sentenced to 45 years in prison. On paper, JOH had been a close US ally in the fight against drugs, as his governments cooperated extensively with Washington on counternarcotics and security. Yet US prosecutors subsequently alleged that he had used the Honduran state and his political power to facilitate the trafficking of more than 400 tonnes of cocaine to the United States in exchange for millions of dollars in bribes. His younger brother, Juan Antonio “Tony” Hernández, a former Honduran congressman, was arrested in 2018, convicted in the United States of cocaine trafficking, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus 30 years.

The pardon acquired a new dimension in 2026 following the publication of a series of leaked recordings known as “Hondurasgate”. The recordings, made between January and April 2026 and published in April, purport to document conversations involving Hernández, Asfura and Vice President María Antonieta Mejía. In the recordings, Hernández claims that individuals linked to Israel, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, were involved in securing and financing his pardon [@hondurasgate2026_israel_joh]. The recordings further allege that Hernández, with support from Republican allies of Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei, discussed establishing a conservative media operation capable of attacking the governments of Gustavo Petro in Colombia and Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico, while planning his own return to the Honduran presidency in exchange for granting the United States a new military base and expanded control over Honduras's special economic zones [@hondurasgate2026_nuevos_audios].

The case therefore illustrates a striking paradox. Hernández was convicted by the US justice system after prosecutors accused him of facilitating hundreds of tonnes of cocaine shipments, yet Trump subsequently pardoned him and backed the candidate of Hernández's own party in a closely contested election. The pardon allowed Hernández to return to Honduras and resume his political influence in the country.

### Mexico

Mexico’s political trajectory since 2000 has been marked by the end of the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s (PRI) long dominance, which lasted continuously from 1929 until 2000, presiding over a one-party-dominant system characterised by patronage and an uneven political playing field. In 2000, Vicente Fox’s victory for the National Action Party (PAN), a generally conservative, centre-right party, ended this 71-year period [@tuckman_2000_mexico_fox_victory]. His successor, fellow PAN politician Felipe Calderón, won the closely contested 2006 election and launched a militarised campaign against drug cartels, contributing to a prolonged escalation in violence. The PRI returned to the presidency in 2012 under Enrique Peña Nieto, whose government pursued market-oriented structural reforms [@tuckman_2012_pri_comeback]. However, the failure of established parties to address persistent security, corruption and poverty problems let to the rise Morena (*Movimiento Regeneración Nacional*, or National Regeneration Movement) and the landslide victory of leftwing populist Andrés Manuel López Obrador in 2018 [@phillips_2018_mexico_despair].

Morena, established as a political movement by López Obrador, widely known as AMLO, represents a break with the established parties, combining a left-wing, redistributive agenda with economic nationalism and a populist political style. AMLO pledged to end what he described as the privileges of the political elite, making the fight against corruption and inequality central to his appeal. His so-called *Fourth Transformation* expanded social programmes, including pensions and scholarships, and oversaw substantial increases in the minimum wage. He also promoted a more interventionist economic model and defended the role of the state in strategic sectors, particularly energy [@phillips_2018_amlo_victory]. His personal popularity and direct communication style, especially through daily morning press conferences, became defining features of his presidency.

In 2024, Mexico became a notable exception to the broader anti-incumbency trend in Latin America, where voters have repeatedly removed governing parties from power, mostly left leaning governments. Barred by the Constitution from running again, López Obrador handed the presidency to a successor from his own party, Claudia Sheinbaum, who won another landslide victory with 59.5 per cent of the presidential vote, thereby becoming Mexico’s first female president and receiving more votes than any previous presidential candidate in the country’s recent history. Sheinbaum has largely continued AMLO’s political project and public style, retaining the emphasis on social programmes, higher wages, state-led development and direct communication with the public. Her background distinguishes her from her predecessor as she trained as a physicist, holds a doctorate in energy engineering and worked as a climate scientist. Her more measured and methodical manner contrasts with López Obrador’s folksier and more confrontational approach, but the political continuity between the two administrations remains clear [@arroyo_2024_sheinbaum_election; @graham_2024_sheinbaum_climate]. Sheinbaum's approval ratings remain very high with 68% of the population considering her performance as positive in August 2026, which makes her one of the world leaders with the highest approval ratings [@mexico_news_daily_2026_sheinbaum_approval_68].

Relations with the United States remain essential but contentious. The US is Mexico’s principal trading partner, and the review of the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) is particularly consequential for its export-oriented economy. Although Donald Trump built part of his political appeal on attacking Mexico, his second administration has increasingly relied on cooperation with President Claudia Sheinbaum. Encounters at the US border had fallen by 87 per cent compared with the final full month of the Biden administration [@nicas_rodriguez_mega_kanno_youngs_2026_trump_mexico_neighbour]. Mexico has also secured comparatively favourable tariff treatment. Although Trump has threatened tariffs against the country, Mexico, which accounts for roughly one-sixth of all US trade, has effectively faced the lowest tariff rate of any major US trading partner [@nicas_rodriguez_mega_kanno_youngs_2026_trump_mexico_neighbour]. Nevertheless, Washington continues to press Mexico to curb migration and drug trafficking while seeking to reduce its trade deficit. Sheinbaum has responded pragmatically, pursuing a trade agreement and exploring increased purchases of US goods, while insisting that cooperation must respect Mexican sovereignty. Tensions persist over US visa revocations targeting Mexican figures accused of links to organised crime and reports of US intelligence activity on Mexican soil. Plans for US airstrikes against cartel targets in Mexico have reportedly been shelved, at least temporarily, amid closer security cooperation. Mexico consequently faces the difficult task of securing favourable trade terms and maintaining security cooperation without appearing to accept US demands at the expense of national sovereignty [@nicas_rodriguez_mega_kanno_youngs_2026_trump_mexico_neighbour].

Mexico’s relationship with China has become more complicated as Washington seeks to limit Beijing’s economic influence in North America. China is a major source of Mexican imports, while the trade relationship is heavily imbalanced in China’s favour. In late 2025, Mexico approved higher tariffs, reaching up to 50 per cent on some products, on imports from countries with which it has no free-trade agreement, including China. The measures, covering a broad range of product categories and taking effect in 2026, were presented by the Mexican government as a means of protecting domestic industry, employment and national production [@reuters_2025_mexico_china_tariffs; @alegria_2025_mexico_tariffs].

Morena appears well positioned to remain competitive in the near term, given Sheinbaum’s high approval ratings, the party’s organisational strength and the weakness of its divided opponents. Mexico’s Constitution prohibits presidential re-election and Sheinbaum will therefore have to leave office in 2030. Morena must identify a successor capable of maintaining its broad electoral coalition and attracting support in their own right, without relying on the personal popularity of either Sheinbaum or López Obrador. The opposition has yet to produce an equally dominant figure. The PAN remains the principal established conservative force, while the PRI, the former ruling party, is considerably weakened.
