### Nicaragua

Nicaragua’s political trajectory since 2000 has been dominated by the return to power of Daniel Ortega and the progressive transformation of the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) from a revolutionary movement into the foundation of an increasingly authoritarian political system. Ortega was one of the leading figures of the Sandinista Revolution, which overthrew the US-backed Somoza dictatorship in 1979. He subsequently led the country as coordinator of the Junta of National Reconstruction and served his first offical term as president from 1985 to 1990. Between 1990 and 2007, Nicaragua was governed by three consecutive center-right administrations. Ortega's return to power in 2007, despite just winning under 38% of the vote, followed a significant pragmatic turn, including an accommodation with conservative former president Arnoldo Alemán through a political pact that helped both leaders strengthen their control over the political system, not least by lowering the threshold for victory in presidential elections. Having initially presented himself as a more moderate candidate, Ortega returned to office promising social programmes and greater inclusion, while maintaining a pragmatic relationship with the private sector and benefiting from support from Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela [@campbell_2001_day_judgment_ortega; @carroll_2009_second_coming_sandinistas].

Once back in power, Ortega progressively weakened institutional checks and balances, restricted political competition and secured the conditions for indefinite re-election. His government initially retained some electoral legitimacy, but the transformation became increasingly apparent as he concentrated control over the judiciary, electoral authorities and state institutions. The decisive rupture came in April 2018, when protests initially triggered by proposed social-security reforms broadened into demands for Ortega’s resignation. The government responded with a violent crackdown that left more than 300 people dead and thousands injured. Repression subsequently expanded to encompass opposition parties, independent media, universities, religious organisations and civil society. In the November 2021 presidential election, leading opposition candidates had been arrested or forced out of the country, and independent political competition was effectively eliminated. Ortega secured another term in an election widely rejected internationally. In September 2026, UN experts concluded that Nicaraguan state institutions had carried out enforced disappearances, torture and arbitrary detention as part of a systematic campaign against political opponents [@hrw_2026_nicaragua].

Ortega’s wife, Rosario Murillo, has become central to this consolidation of power. Having served as his campaign communications chief in 2001 and subsequently as the government’s principal spokesperson, she became vice-president in 2017. A constitutional overhaul that entered into force in February 2025 formally established a co-presidency, making Murillo co-president alongside her husband and providing a constitutional framework for dynastic succession. The reform also concentrated power in the executive, subordinating other state institutions to the presidency and extending the presidential term from five to six years. Nicaraguan outlet *Confidencial* has reported that Murillo increasingly directs the government’s day-to-day operations, including political appointments, party organisation, communications and relations with foreign partners, while Ortega’s role has become more ceremonial. The couple’s children also occupy influential positions in government, investment promotion and state-aligned media, reinforcing the increasingly familial character of the system [@confidencial_2026_rosario_murillo_power].

The authoritarian consolidation has continued in 2026. Ortega publicly declared in July that Nicaragua would hold no further elections, to prevent the opposition from "seizing the government" again. In September, the National Assembly approved the first vote on a further constitutional amendment that would extend presidential and other elected terms from six to seven years and prohibit opposition parties from participating in elections. These developments point towards the further institutionalisation of a system in which electoral competition would no longer constitute a meaningful route to political change [@reuters_2026_nicaragua_reform_opposition_elections; @nicas_wagner_2026_ortega_abolish_elections].

Relations with the United States and Western governments have deteriorated in parallel with the domestic crackdown. Washington has imposed successive sanctions on Nicaraguan officials and regime-linked businesses, while European governments have also taken restrictive measures over human-rights violations. In April 2026, the US Treasury Department sanctioned two of the presidential couple’s sons, alongside officials and companies linked to the gold sector and the seizure of US-owned property. In October, the Ortega–Murillo government rejected the appointment of Natasha Franceschi as the next US ambassador. Washington subsequently recalled its chargé d’affaires, Elias Baumann, to the United States for consultations, deepening a diplomatic crisis that had already left the country without a US ambassador for several years [@us_treasury_2026_nicaragua_gold_sanctions; @reuters_2026_us_nicaragua_ambassador_rejected].

Nicaragua increasingly finds itself in international self isolation. In January 2026, Nicaragua expelled Spanish ambassador Sergio Farré Salvá and the embassy’s second-ranking diplomat without publicly explaining the decision. Spain responded by expelling Nicaragua’s ambassador in Madrid and another Nicaraguan diplomat in application of strict reciprocity. The incident followed several years of deteriorating relations, during which Managua has expelled or obstructed the work of foreign diplomats and international organisations, including representatives of the European Union and other Western countries. Nicaragua has also expelled numerous international organisations, ranging from the Organisation of American States and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to the Food and Agriculture Organisation and the International Committee of the Red Cross [@pinell_2026_nicaragua_expels_spain_ambassador; @gonzalez_2026_spain_nicaragua_ambassadors].

Against this backdrop, Nicaragua has sought to strengthen relations with China and Russia. In December 2021, Managua restored diplomatic relations with Beijing, abandoning its longstanding diplomatic recognition of Taiwan in favour of the People’s Republic of China. The two countries subsequently elevated their relationship to a strategic partnership, and a bilateral free-trade agreement entered into force in January 2024 [@china_mfa_2021_nicaragua_relations; @cash_2023_nicaragua_china_ties]. Russia’s role is more explicitly strategic and security-oriented. Moscow has continued to provide political backing for Ortega and maintained long-standing military ties dating back to the first Sandinista government during the Cold War [@reuters_2024_patrushev_nicaragua].

Nicaragua’s geopolitical position must also be understood in the context of the weakening of the regional alignment that once challenged US influence. Ortega’s government has long been part of the Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America (ALBA), alongside Cuba and Venezuela, and has presented itself as a defender of sovereignty against US interventionism. The removal of Nicolás Maduro by US forces in January 2026 and the subsequent engagement between Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, and Washington have significantly weakened this political alignment. Cuba, meanwhile, faces acute economic and energy pressures. Although these governments were never a fully coherent bloc, Nicaragua and Cuba now stand out as among the region’s most consistently confrontational governments towards Washington. China and Russia provide Managua with diplomatic and security support, but the weakening of its regional allies leaves Nicaragua more isolated [@chamorro_2026_nicaragua_cuba_venezuela].

### Panama

José Raúl Mulino has been president of Panama since July 2024, when he took office after winning the May presidential election with 34.3% of the vote. Mulino had originally been running as the vice-presidential candidate of former president Ricardo Martinelli, who was constitutionally barred from standing after being convicted of money laundering. Martinelli nevertheless remained central to the campaign, and Mulino's victory was largely built on his political support and the promise of returning to the economic policies associated with his presidency. Mulino has since pursued a broadly pro-business and security-oriented agenda, while facing the economic consequences of the closure of the Cobre Panamá copper mine and continuing concerns over migration through the Darién Gap.

Relations with the United States have strengthened considerably under Mulino, particularly on security, migration and the Panama Canal. The military dimension of this cooperation has come into focus as in October 2026 it was reported that the first elements of a 600-soldier US Army battalion had begun deploying to a jungle-training facility in Panama, ahead of planned exercises with forces in Colombia and Honduras [@schmitt_jaffe_correal_2026_us_troops_latin_america]. The US Embassy in Panama disputed the reported deployment, stating that 120 US soldiers were attending a two-week training course and would return to the United States on 25 October [@us_embassy_panama_2026_troop_training]. Panama has cooperated closely with Washington on controlling migration through the Darién and combating drug trafficking, while the Trump administration has placed increasing emphasis on reducing Chinese influence around the Canal. In 2025, Panama announced that it would withdraw from China's Belt and Road Initiative, becoming the first Latin American country to do so. Mulino also agreed to increased US military cooperation and to accept migrants deported from the United States. These agreements generated domestic controversy as former president Martín Torrijos and former presidential candidate Ricardo Lombana joined other critics in arguing that the arrangements threatened Panamanian sovereignty. Both subsequently had their US visas revoked, although the State Department did not explain the individual decisions [@robles_2025_panama_torrijos_visa]. Mulino has nevertheless repeatedly rejected claims that China controls the Canal, stressing that the waterway remains under Panamanian sovereignty.

The most important manifestation of the US-China rivalry in Panama has been the controversy surrounding the ports at the two entrances to the Canal. Since 1997, Balboa on the Pacific side and Cristóbal on the Atlantic side had been operated by Panama Ports Company (PPC), a subsidiary of the Hong Kong-based conglomerate CK Hutchison Holdings. Although the ports are separate from the Canal itself, their strategic location made their operation a major concern for Washington. In 2025, Panama's Controller General accused CK Hutchison of failing to properly renew its concession and of owing the state \$300 million in fees. The dispute coincided with CK Hutchison's proposed \$19 billion sale of its global port business, including the two Panamanian terminals, to a consortium led by BlackRock. The proposed sale was welcomed by Washington but strongly criticised by Beijing, turning the ports into a focal point of the broader US-China rivalry [@eavis_2025_panama_ports_misconduct].

In January 2026, Panama's Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the legal framework underlying PPC's concession. Following publication of the ruling in February, the Panamanian authorities took control of the two terminals, with Mulino insisting that this did not constitute an expropriation but the implementation of a binding judicial decision [@la_prensa_2026_panama_ports]. CK Hutchison and PPC rejected the termination and reserved their right to pursue legal action, while Beijing said it would take measures to protect the legitimate interests of Chinese companies [@la_estrella_2026_panama_ports]. The dispute therefore acquired an increasingly geopolitical dimension, with Panama caught between US pressure to reduce Chinese strategic influence and the importance of maintaining its economic relationship with China.

The port dispute has not, however, resulted in a complete rupture with Beijing. China is an important trading partner and major user of the Canal, while Chinese companies have invested extensively in Panama since diplomatic relations were established in 2017. Mulino has sought to preserve these economic ties while defending Panama's decision on the ports. In February, he argued that China itself depended heavily on Panama because Chinese goods pass through the Canal and the country's logistics infrastructure [@la_estrella_2026_mulino_china]. In April, tensions increased further when Panama reported that dozens of Panama-flagged vessels had been detained in China. Mulino sought to de-escalate the dispute while investigating the detentions [@la_estrella_2026_detentions]. The episode illustrates that Panama's closer strategic alignment with Washington has not eliminated its substantial economic interdependence with China.

Panama under Mulino therefore represents a clear case of closer strategic alignment with the United States, particularly on security, migration and strategically sensitive infrastructure, accompanied by a significant reduction in its engagement with China. At the same time, Mulino has continued to emphasise Panamanian sovereignty and sought to avoid a broader rupture with Beijing. The controversy over the CK Hutchison ports illustrates how US-China competition is increasingly shaping political and economic decisions in Latin America, particularly where Chinese commercial interests intersect with infrastructure of strategic importance to Washington.

### Paraguay

Paraguay’s political trajectory since 2000 has been characterised by continuity rather than the alternation between left and right seen elsewhere in Latin America. The conservative Colorado Party governed uninterruptedly from 1947, including throughout Alfredo Stroessner’s dictatorship, until 2008 when Fernando Lugo came to power as the first former Catholic bishop to assume the presidency of a country in the region [@nickson_2008_paraguay_giro_izquierda_lugo]. Lugo was removed through a contentious impeachment process in 2012 and his Vice-President Federico Franco took over for the remaining year of the mandate. Since then, the Colorado Party has been in power again uninterruptedly.

In the 2023 general election, the Colorado Party’s candidate Santiago Peña, a former finance minister and International Monetary Fund economist, won approximately 43 per cent of the vote, defeating centre-left opposition candidate Efraín Alegre. The elections took place in a highly polarised environment marked by deep distrust in state institutions [@eu_eom_2023_paraguay; @elliott_desantis_2023_paraguay_pena_cartes].

Peña’s presidency has been closely associated with former president Horacio Cartes, who remains one of the country’s most influential political figures. Cartes had sought to amend the constitution in 2017 to allow himself an additional term, but was forced to abandon his plans following widespread street protests, as the constitution has prohibited presidential re-election since 1992 following the fall of Stroessner’s military government, which lasted from 1954 to 1989 [@bbc_mundo_2017_paraguay_reeleccion]. He subsequently selected Peña as his preferred successor and backed his successful presidential campaign. Although Peña presents himself as a technocratic, pro-business leader focused on economic growth and foreign investment, critics have questioned his autonomy from Cartes. In January 2023, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Cartes and former Vice-President Hugo Adalberto Velázquez Moreno "for their involvement in the rampant corruption that undermines democratic institutions in Paraguay" [@us_treasury_2023_paraguay_cartes_velazquez_sanctions]. The Trump administration lifted the sanctions in October 2025, and Peña welcomed the decision as an improvement in bilateral relations. Opposition figures attributed the reversal to a series of pro-US foreign policy decisions, including an agreement to receive asylum seekers from the United States and Paraguay’s participation in Trump’s Shield of the Americas initiative, which Peña signed on 7 March 2026 at the inaugural summit held in Doral, Florida. A US State Department spokesperson stated that the sanctions were “no longer required to incentivise changes in behaviour, and therefore not in the foreign policy and national security interests of the United States” [@ofac_2025_cartes_sanctions_removal; @blair_2025_cartes_sanctions_scrapped; @reuters_2025_cartes_sanctions_lift].

Concerns about institutional accountability have persisted under Peña. In February 2024, allies of Cartes in the Senate helped expel opposition senator Kattya González over alleged administrative misconduct, a decision that rights groups criticised as a violation of due process. Later that year, legislation imposing extensive reporting requirements on non-governmental organisations entered into force, raising concerns among opposition parties, UN experts, and civil society organisations that the law would effectively allow the government to persecute groups it considered hostile [@freedom_house_2025_paraguay].

The October 2026 municipal elections provided an early indication of the challenges facing the governing party ahead of the 2028 general election. The Colorado Party retained its nationwide dominance and increased the number of municipalities under its control compared with 2021, but suffered significant defeats in Asunción, the capital, and Ciudad del Este, the country’s second-largest city. In Asunción, opposition candidate Soledad Núñez won 47.78 per cent of the vote against 45.98 per cent for the Colorado candidate. Núñez had been the running mate of Efraín Alegre of the Liberal Party in his unsuccessful 2023 presidential bid. These results do not amount to a national realignment, but they expose vulnerabilities in the governing party’s electoral machinery and offer the opposition an opportunity to build a more credible challenge ahead of 2028 [@desantis_2026_paraguay_municipal; @efe_2026_paraguay_municipal].

One of the most consequential aspects of Paraguay’s foreign policy is its continued diplomatic recognition of Taiwan. Paraguay is the only remaining country in South America and one of just twelve worldwide to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Under Peña, the government has repeatedly reaffirmed this commitment, including during his visit to Taipei in May 2026. The relationship encompasses cooperation in education, technology, and security, as well as access for Paraguayan agricultural exports to the Taiwanese market. However, the Taiwanese market cannot compete with the Chinese one, and there is growing pressure from Paraguayan farmers to abandon the relationship with Taipei and establish formal ties with Beijing [@elliott_desantis_2023_paraguay_pena_cartes]. Despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations, Paraguay maintains substantial trade with China, valued at approximately \$5 billion in 2024. Paraguayan officials have indicated openness to commercial and other relations with Beijing, but have stated they will not accept the condition of severing ties with Taiwan [@johnson_wu_2024_paraguay_taiwan_china].

The dispute intensified in October 2026 when China imposed sanctions on Paraguay’s Minister of Information and Communication Technologies, Gustavo Villate, and Belize’s foreign minister over their countries’ continued ties with Taiwan. Beijing accused the officials of supporting Taiwan’s independence and spreading disinformation about Chinese cyberattacks. The measures included asset freezes in China, entry restrictions, and a ban on Chinese organisations and individuals cooperating with the sanctioned officials; their practical impact is largely symbolic [@reuters_2026_china_sanctions_paraguay_taiwan]. Paraguay rejected the sanctions and reiterated its support for Taiwan, while the US State Department condemned them as coercive measures against countries exercising their sovereign foreign-policy choices [@abc_color_2026_paraguay_china_sanctions; @reuters_2026_us_china_coercion_paraguay].

### Peru

Peru’s political trajectory since 2000 has been marked by the collapse of Alberto Fujimori’s authoritarian government, an initially promising democratic transition and, more recently, chronic presidential instability. Fujimori fled the country in November 2000 amid a corruption scandal that exposed the systematic bribery of politicians and other public figures by his intelligence chief, Vladimiro Montesinos. His departure ushered in a transitional administration under Valentín Paniagua, followed by the election of Alejandro Toledo in 2001. Toledo, Alan García (2006–2011) and Ollanta Humala (2011–2016) all completed their presidential terms, but successive corruption scandals, including the far-reaching Odebrecht affair, undermined public confidence in the political establishment. Fujimori’s legacy also remained influential as his daughter Keiko emerged as the leading figure of *fujimorismo*, the political movement associated with her father’s rule, and became one of the most prominent conservative politicians in the country [@collyns_jones_2024_fujimori_legacy; @gomez_vega_2025_ultimos_11_presidentes].

The breakdown in presidential stability accelerated after Pedro Pablo Kuczynski took office in 2016. He resigned in March 2018 amid an escalating impeachment crisis linked to allegations concerning the Odebrecht corruption scandal. His successor, Martín Vizcarra, was removed by Congress in November 2020, triggering mass protests that forced interim president Manuel Merino to resign after just five days. Francisco Sagasti then served as a caretaker president until the 2021 election, won by left-wing outsider Pedro Castillo. Castillo’s confrontation with Congress culminated in December 2022, when he attempted to dissolve the legislature and govern by decree; Congress removed him and he was arrested on rebellion charges and sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2025. His vice-president, Dina Boluarte, succeeded him but was eventually removed in October 2025 amid mounting insecurity, protests and political scandals. Her successors, José Jerí and interim president José María Balcázar, further illustrated the fragility of the executive as Jerí was removed after four months, while Balcázar held office until the inauguration of the newly elected president in July 2026. Peru had thus experienced nine presidencies in roughly a decade, reflecting the combination of fragmented parties, minority governments, corruption scandals and recurrent conflict between Congress and the executive [@roy_2026_peru_ninth_president_decade; @gomez_vega_2025_ultimos_11_presidentes].

Against this backdrop, the June 2026 presidential run-off brought *fujimorismo* back to power a quarter of a century after the collapse of Alberto Fujimori’s government. After three unsuccessful presidential campaigns, Keiko Fujimori defeated left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez by just 49,641 votes, becoming the first woman elected directly to Peru’s presidency. Her victory was nevertheless unusual as she received fewer votes than Sánchez within Peru itself, with the overseas vote tipping the national result in her favour [@eu_eom_2026_peru; @glatsky_2026_peru_china]. The return of *fujimorismo* also creates an evident political irony. Over the preceding decade, *Fuerza Popular*, the party led by incumbent president Fujimori, alone or in alliance with other parties, participated in the removals of four presidents: Martín Vizcarra, Pedro Castillo, Dina Boluarte and José Jerí. The movement that had repeatedly used its influence in Congress to undermine other presidents must now govern without a legislative majority of its own [@zambrano_2026_keiko_fujimori_congress_limits].

The limits of that power have already become apparent. Fuerza Popular holds only 41 of the 130 seats in the lower chamber, forcing the government to negotiate with other parties to pass legislation. In October 2026, Congress substantially curtailed Fujimori’s request for temporary powers to legislate by decree as of the 66 measures proposed by the government, only 20 were approved, and the authorisation period was shortened from 120 to 90 days. Even some parties previously regarded as allies opposed the government’s proposals, including its request to give the armed forces a greater role in prison security [@zambrano_2026_keiko_fujimori_congress_limits]. Her popularity has also fallen sharply. According to recent polling, her approval rating dropped by 14.5 percentage points to 28.3 per cent in early October 2026, while disapproval rose to 53.6 per cent [@bloomberg_news_2026_fujimori_approval_sinks]. These early difficulties suggest that winning the presidency has not resolved the structural problems that have repeatedly destabilised Peruvian governments. As under her predecessors, Fujimori must contend with a fragmented legislature, widespread distrust of political institutions and public expectations that may prove difficult to meet.

The change of government has also brought a shift in foreign policy orientation. The clearest signal is the appointment of Carlos Espá as Foreign Minister. Having served as communications director in the press and culture department of the US Embassy in Lima from 2008 to 2023, Espá confirmed upon taking office that Peru would join Trump's Shield of the Americas coalition as part of Fujimori's security agenda, describing the United States as a "strategic partner." Relations with China, however, are unlikely to undergo any dramatic change, given Beijing's centrality to the Peruvian economy. China has become Peru's largest trading partner and a major investor in mining, energy, and infrastructure. When the 2008 financial crisis depressed US and European demand for minerals, China's construction boom continued to absorb Peruvian copper and iron, and Beijing eventually surpassed Washington as Lima's principal trading partner, today purchasing roughly a third of the country's exports. Beyond trade, Chinese state-owned enterprises have steadily expanded into sectors from which Western businesses have retreated, including Lima's electricity distribution system, as well as transportation, banking, and telecommunications [@glatsky_2026_peru_china].

China also financed the \$1.3 billion Chancay mega-port north of Lima, which has become a particular concern for Washington. The port was a key issue during Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Peru in August 2026, as part of the Trump administration's broader efforts to roll back Chinese influence in the Western Hemisphere [@glatsky_2026_peru_china]. In September 2026, the US State Department announced visa revocations targeting several current and former officials from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru [@state_department_2026_visa_restrictions]. The only Peruvian national targeted was judge Juan Carlos Nuñez Matos, who had ruled in a case concerning the Chancay port that it constituted a private investment rather than a state concession. The ruling was opposed by the United States because it limited the regulatory oversight that could be exercised over the port [@cepr_2026_us_escalation]. The State Department did not provide evidence or further details explaining the reasons for the visa revocation, but its timing and the judge's involvement in the Chancay case raise the possibility that the two were connected.

The contrast in the nature of US and Chinese engagement with Peru is striking. While China has channelled investment into ports, mines, and electricity infrastructure, US engagement has focused predominantly on security cooperation funded by Peru itself, including a \$1.5 billion modernisation of the country's naval base and the purchase of 24 F-16 fighter jets at a cost of \$3.5 billion [@glatsky_2026_peru_china].

### Uruguay

Uruguay’s political trajectory since 2000 stands out in Latin America for the stability of its democratic institutions and the peaceful alternation of power between the left and the right. In the early 2000s, a severe financial crisis, compounded by Argentina’s economic collapse, undermined confidence in the traditional Colorado and National parties. The centre-left Broad Front (*Frente Amplio*) capitalised on this discontent to win the 2004 presidential election, bringing Tabaré Vázquez to power in 2005 and ending more than a century of political dominance by the traditional parties. Subsequent Broad Front governments under José Mujica (2010–2015) and Vázquez again (2015–2020) expanded social protection and introduced progressive reforms, including the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage and the state-regulated production and sale of cannabis [@baldock_2004_uruguay_first_left; @cariboni_2014_uruguay_social_reforms; @rivas_molina_2024_uruguay_democracy_tranquila].

The Broad Front lost the presidency in 2019 to Luis Lacalle Pou’s centre-right coalition, which governed from 2020 to 2025. In November 2024, however, Broad Front candidate Yamandú Orsi defeated Álvaro Delgado, the candidate of the outgoing coalition, and took office on 1 March 2025. True to Uruguay’s tradition of peaceful alternation, Lacalle Pou promptly recognised Orsi’s victory, and both camps pledged to cooperate during the transition. The campaign was comparatively moderate by regional standards, with established parties retaining their identities and political outsiders making little headway. Yet the result was not simply a return to the left after a temporary right-wing interlude. The Broad Front rebuilt its support through extensive local campaigning and by capitalising on dissatisfaction with the government’s record on crime and social problems, as well as scandals involving senior officials [@guardian_2024_uruguay_orsi_election; @rivas_molina_2024_uruguay_campaign_discontent].

Uruguay’s relative stability should not obscure persistent social divisions. Poverty and inequality remain unevenly distributed, with children disproportionately affected, while violent crime and concerns about education and the cost of living have become more prominent in public debate. These concerns helped shape the 2024 election despite the country’s comparatively robust social protection system and macroeconomic track record. Orsi has presented his programme as a “modern left”: continuing the Broad Front’s commitment to redistribution, while avoiding a sharp policy rupture and maintaining economic stability. His government must now demonstrate that Uruguay’s institutional stability can translate into tangible improvements for the social groups that have benefited least from previous progress [@rivas_molina_2024_uruguay_democracy_tranquila; @guardian_2024_uruguay_orsi_election].

Relations with the United States illustrate the pragmatic and sometimes uncomfortable character of Uruguay’s foreign policy. Orsi’s centre-left government has maintained dialogue with Washington, but it has not been immune to pressure from the Trump administration. In July 2026, it was reported that the US was seeking to use Uruguay as a destination for Cuban nationals deported from the United States, describing negotiations as close to an agreement. Uruguay had its own reasons to engage in negotiations. As a country with a historically open immigration policy and a small, ageing population in need of immigrant workers, it stood to benefit from the arrangement while simultaneously improving relations with the Trump administration [@wong_bubola_2026_trump_cuban_deportees_uruguay]. Uruguay was not among the countries invited to join Trump’s *Shield of the Americas*, launched in March 2026. President Orsi described the omission as surprising and said Uruguay was willing to cooperate on combating drug trafficking and organised crime. He proposed addressing these issues through the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC), bringing all countries into the coordination effort rather than relying on a selective coalition [@elpais_uy_2026_orsi_shield_americas; @telenoche_2026_orsi_celac_security].

China was Uruguay’s largest destination for goods exports in 2025, accounting for approximately 26 per cent of the total, with agricultural commodities central to the relationship. Orsi’s state visit to China in February 2026 brought a 150-person delegation of ministers, officials, business representatives, trade unionists and academics, underscoring that the relationship extends beyond presidential diplomacy. During the visit, Orsi also announced that Uruguay intended to seek accession to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), a trade agreement among 15 Asia-Pacific economies that together account for approximately 30 per cent of global GDP [@asean_2020_rcep_summary]. The government presented the initiative as part of a wider effort to open markets and diversify trade, including improving access for products such as poultry and dairy. It should not be read as evidence of a straightforward geopolitical shift towards Beijing. Uruguay has an established interest in the Chinese market, and the pursuit of wider Asian trade links has also featured under previous governments. Nevertheless, the RCEP initiative raises practical questions, including how Uruguay’s ambition for greater trade autonomy would fit with Mercosur’s common commercial policy [@uruguay_xxi_2026_exports_china; @chu_2026_uruguay_rcep; @la_diaria_2026_orsi_china_visit].

Relations with the European Union provide another route for diversification. The EU–Mercosur agreement, signed in January 2026 after more than two decades of negotiations, began provisional application of its trade provisions on 1 May. Orsi and his foreign minister have presented it as an opportunity to expand trade and investment and strengthen ties with a major partner beyond the United States and China. However, the agreement is not without complications. As of June 2026, Mercosur members had still not agreed how to distribute some of the export quotas negotiated with the EU, exposing tensions over how the benefits of integration should be shared. For Uruguay, the deal offers valuable market access, but its benefits will depend on how the country captures a fair share of the quotas and whether increased trade volumes translate into broader industrial and productive development [@centenera_2026_eu_mercosur_signing; @galarraga_colman_2026_mercosur_asia; @rivas_molina_2026_lubetkin_uruguay_foreign_policy].

Mercosur remains both an instrument of influence and a constraint on Uruguay’s ambitions. As a small economy, Uruguay benefits from negotiating with larger partners as part of a regional bloc, yet successive governments have sought more flexibility to pursue trade opportunities independently. Under Orsi, the government has continued to advocate a more open and outward-looking Mercosur and has shown interest in exploring additional agreements with Asian partners. These aims place Uruguay between competing approaches within the bloc as Brazil stresses regional cohesion, while Argentina under Javier Milei has pushed more forcefully for freedom to negotiate bilateral deals. Orsi’s position has been closer to the argument for greater flexibility, but without abandoning Mercosur. This reflects a recurring dilemma for Uruguay where integration increases its collective leverage, yet restrictive common rules can limit its ability to respond quickly to opportunities in global markets [@galarraga_colman_2026_mercosur_asia; @rivas_molina_2026_lubetkin_uruguay_foreign_policy].

In a regional environment increasingly shaped by right-wing governments and sharper geopolitical competition, Uruguay remains one of the relatively few centre-left administrations. Its foreign policy, however, is not organised around an anti-US bloc or an exclusive alignment with China. Instead, the government seeks to maintain workable relations with Washington, deepen commercial links with Beijing, strengthen the partnership with Europe and use Mercosur to widen its room for manoeuvre. The central tension is whether Uruguay can sustain this multi-directional approach when its partners increasingly seek political alignment as well as economic cooperation.

### Venezuela

The US military operation *Absolute Resolve*, launched on 3 January 2026, represents a watershed moment for Venezuela and the wider region. It marks the first time in recent history that the United States has captured a sitting head of state and transferred him to US soil to face trial, with Nicolás Maduro now detained in Manhattan awaiting proceedings. By establishing provisional authorities drawn from within the Chavista regime but approved by Washington, the United States transformed a country that had been a strategic adversary into something resembling a client state [@elliott2026venezuela].

The provisionality of these authorities, however, remains an open and deeply consequential question, as no democratic elections are foreseen in the near future. While many Venezuelans had long hoped for external assistance to remove their autocratic leader, the intervention has come at a significant cost.

On 31 August 2026, the White House announced that it had secured majority US control over more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves [@whitehouse2026_venezuela_oil]. Venezuela is believed to possess the world’s largest oil reserves. What is particularly striking is that the country appears to have ceded control over its principal natural resource through a profoundly asymmetric arrangement to a private company run by an oligarch who made his fortune under Chavismo and is now firmly subordinated to US power. The company is partly owned by the US government, which exercises near-total control over its board of directors, while its contracts are governed by US law and subject to US courts. Indeed, since the era of decolonisation, no oil-producing country has surrendered its principal resources under comparable conditions [@legrandcontinent2026_venezuela_recolonisation].

The interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, has emphasised the substantial financial resources that the Venezuelan state stands to receive from the agreement. A figure of \$200 billion has been cited, to be transferred over 25 years. Although this sum appears substantial, \$200 billion spread over 25 years amounts to approximately \$8 billion per year. Assuming production of between 2 and 2.5 million barrels per day, this would represent a state take of roughly \$10 per barrel. That figure falls well below the level suggested by international benchmarks, under which a host state typically receives between 50 and 90 per cent of profits. Moreover, much of the promised \$200 billion would reportedly be paid in the distant future, when production reaches its peak [@legrandcontinent2026_venezuela_recolonisation].

Rather than using its leverage first to re-establish constitutional rule and democracy in Venezuela, and then negotiating with a legitimate government capable of making credible long-term commitments, the United States appears to have prioritised the acquisition of strategic assets. Rodríguez lacks both democratic legitimacy and the political credibility required to govern the country, while the agreement is contested by large sections of the Venezuelan population. Should democratic elections eventually produce a change of government, the arrangement could be challenged, potentially giving the United States a structural incentive to delay a genuine political transition. This dynamic is illustrated by the situation of opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who has attempted to return to Venezuela from Panama on seven occasions, each time thwarted by a combination of technical failures, denied permits, and the refusal of neighbouring countries to grant passage, while Washington insists she is free to do so [@alandete2026_machado_venezuela]. After then months in exile, she eventually returned to Venezuela on 25 October 2025 [@aljazeera_2026_machado_return; @machado_2026_x_return]. At the UN General Assembly in September 2026, Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez vowed that there will be elections without setting a date or offer electoral guarantees [@turkewitz2026_rodriguez_unga].

At the centre of the agreement is Lorenzo Betancourt, whose company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), has reportedly been granted 100-year concessions to operate 17 oil fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves, roughly equivalent to the total proven reserves of the United States [@romero2026_Betancourt]. Betancourt does not own the fields outright, but the concessions grant him exclusive exploitation rights. The arrangement is particularly striking in light of his legal history. Legal proceedings were initiated against him in Spain and Switzerland on money-laundering charges, and both countries requested his extradition from the United Kingdom, where he lives on a 14-bedroom country estate. British authorities arrested him less than a year ago and barred him from travelling abroad. Under the agreement between NABEP and the United States, the Pentagon holds a significant equity stake in the company. The arrangement is difficult to compare with any recent precedent in American history and places Betancourt at the centre of Venezuela’s transformation from a sovereign state into what critics describe as a vassal of the United States [@romero2026_Betancourt].

The White House acknowledged in its fact sheet that most of the oil fields to be operated by NABEP were previously controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese firms [@whitehouse2026_venezuela_oil]. A document reviewed by *The New York Times* showed that China Concord Petroleum was participating in at least two of the 17 areas as recently as 2024. The company had been placed under US sanctions in 2019 for its alleged involvement in transporting Iranian oil. China’s foreign ministry responded that “China’s legitimate rights and interests in Venezuela must be guaranteed” [@elliott2026_NYT]. Both China and Russia, which once exercised considerable influence in Venezuela, now appear to have limited leverage to alter the country’s new trajectory.
